title: Made Like His Brothers: The Son Who Tasted Death
summary: Because the Son is so great, his readers must not drift from the salvation he announced. The author then turns to Psalm 8: God made humanity to rule over all things, and though we do not yet see that, we see Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while, crowned with glory because he suffered death for everyone. He shared our flesh and blood to destroy the devil's power, free those enslaved by fear of death, and become a merciful and faithful high priest.
story: Chapter 1 showed the Son above the angels. Chapter 2 does two things with that. First, it draws the practical conclusion in the first of the letter's five warnings (verses 1-4): if the law delivered through angels carried penalties, how much more the salvation announced by the Lord himself. Second, it faces an obvious objection. If the Son is so exalted, why did he suffer and die? The answer is that he came down below the angels, into human life, on purpose. The chapter introduces the title that will dominate the middle of the book, high priest (verse 17), and explains why only a human being could fill it.
historical:
Verse 3 is one of the few windows into the author's own situation. The salvation was announced by the Lord and "confirmed to us by those who heard Him", which places the author and readers among the second generation of believers who received the gospel from eyewitnesses. That detail is one reason many interpreters, from early centuries onward, doubted that Paul wrote Hebrews, since Paul insisted he received his gospel directly from Christ (Galatians 1:12). Verse 4 recalls the signs, wonders, and gifts of the Spirit that accompanied the early preaching, as Acts describes.

The belief that the law was given through angels (verse 2) does not come from Exodus, which does not mention them at Sinai, but it was widespread in Jewish tradition. The Greek version of Deuteronomy 33:2 speaks of angels with God at Sinai, and Stephen and Paul both mention the idea (Acts 7:53, Galatians 3:19).
cultural:
Fear of death shaped the ancient world. Funeral inscriptions often expressed bleak resignation, and philosophers such as the Epicureans and Stoics offered arguments meant to free people from that fear. Verse 15 describes humanity as held in lifelong slavery to it and names the devil as the one who wields the power of death, drawing on the story of Genesis 3, where death enters through the serpent's deception.

Kinship obligations mattered enormously. A family member had duties to redeem relatives from debt or slavery, avenge their blood, and care for them; the Old Testament calls such a person a kinsman-redeemer. The author's stress that the Son and his people are "of the same family" and that he is "not ashamed to call them brothers" (verse 11) implies that he takes on those obligations. The word translated author or founder in verse 10 was used of a pioneer or champion who leads others into new territory.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-4 are a warning built as an argument from lesser to greater, a standard pattern in Jewish interpretation: if the lesser thing is true, the greater must be even more so. Verses 5-18 are an exposition of Psalm 8:4-6, which in its original setting praises God for giving frail human beings rule over creation. The author reads it in two stages. Humanity was meant to have all things under its feet, but "at present we do not see everything subject to him" (verse 8). What we do see is Jesus, who has taken the path the psalm describes, lowered and then crowned. Three more quotations, from Psalm 22:22 and Isaiah 8:17-18, put words in Jesus' mouth to show his solidarity with his people. The chapter ends with two purpose statements (verses 14-15 and 17-18) that explain why he had to become like us: to break death's power and to serve as a merciful priest.

outline.t: Warning: do not drift from so great a salvation
Psalm 8: humanity's destiny fulfilled in Jesus
The founder of salvation calls them brothers
Sharing flesh and blood to destroy death's power
A merciful and faithful high priest

doctrines.note: Jesus is fully human, sharing flesh and blood, suffering, and being tempted. The church later confessed that he is truly God and truly man; Hebrews 1 and 2 stand side by side as the two halves of that confession.

By his death Jesus tastes death for everyone, destroys the one who held death's power, frees captives, and makes atonement for the sins of the people (verses 9, 14-15, 17). The chapter joins the ideas of victory over evil and of sacrifice for sin.

Psalm 8 describes the dignity and calling of every human being, made a little lower than the angels and crowned to rule. That calling has not been lost, but it is now realized in Jesus and, through him, in the many sons and daughters he brings to glory.
Jesus was made perfect through suffering and is able to help those who are tested because he was tested himself. Suffering is not a sign of God's absence but the road the Son himself walked.

words.note: Pararreo, to drift away or flow past, a word used of a boat slipping past its harbor or a ring slipping off a finger. The danger the author fears is not a dramatic rejection but a slow, unnoticed drift away from what the readers have heard (verse 1).

Archegos, founder, pioneer, champion, or leader. It describes someone who goes first and opens a way for others to follow. Jesus is the archegos of salvation who leads many sons to glory (verse 10), and in 12:2 he is the founder of faith.

Teleioo, to make perfect or complete, to bring to the intended goal. When Hebrews says the Son was made perfect through suffering, it does not mean he was morally flawed. It means he was fully qualified for his office as savior and priest by completing the path of obedience and suffering.

Hilaskomai, to make atonement or propitiation, to deal with sin so that it no longer stands between God and people. In the Greek Old Testament the related noun names the mercy seat on the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Jesus as high priest makes this atonement for his people (verse 17).

christ: This chapter presents Jesus as the true human being. Psalm 8 describes what humanity was made to be, and Jesus is the one in whom that vocation is fulfilled. He came lower than the angels, tasted death, and was crowned with glory and honor. He does it not for himself but as the elder brother of a family, bringing "many sons to glory" (verse 10). He shares our nature so that by his death he can destroy the one "who holds the power of death" and free those enslaved by its fear. And because he was tested and suffered, he is "a merciful and faithful high priest" who can help those who are being tested now.

hard.q: If Jesus was the eternal Son, how could God make him "perfect through suffering"?
hard.a:
The phrase sounds as if Jesus had faults to overcome, but the letter itself rules that out: he was tempted "yet was without sin" (4:15), and he is holy and innocent (7:26). In Hebrews the language of perfection means completion or being brought to a goal. In the Greek Old Testament the same word group is used for the consecration of priests into their office. Jesus was made perfect in the sense that his suffering and obedience completed his qualification to be the savior and high priest of his people. He did not become more divine or more good; he became, through experience, the fully tested human priest who can sympathize with others.

Theologians have also noted that the eternal Son took on a real human life that grew and developed (Luke 2:52 says he increased in wisdom). Growth and learning belong to his genuine humanity, and the church has held that this does not diminish his deity.

questions: The author worries more about drifting than about open rebellion. What slow currents tend to pull people away from what they believe?
Jesus is "not ashamed to call them brothers". How does it change your picture of him to think of him as an elder brother who shares your family?
Verse 18 says Jesus can help those who are being tempted because he was tempted himself. Where would that help matter most in your life right now?
